clue.text: 25 put up in space, not entirely a king

indicators.note: in places the turned word for put inside the shortened word for space
only part of the word for space is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a room is a space, as in 'no room to move'

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for put is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: to lay something is to put it down
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Something is put up in a space, and it is not quite a king.
explanation.walkthrough: '25' points to the answer to 25-across, a pub. 'not entirely' drops the last letter of the word for space; 'up' turns the word for put backwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Oak is one of the commonest British pub names, so it is an example of a pub.

clue.text: 25 country virtually European in order of clues

indicators.note: in places the shortened country and the European inside the rearranged letters of clues
putting the letters of clues into a new order signals an anagram
virtually means almost, so the country's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Uganda is an African country
a Lett is a Latvian, a European people

explanation.surface: A pub somewhere in a nearly European country, listed in the order the clues appear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order of' rearranges the letters of clues; the nearly complete country and the Latvian sit 'in' between them. 'order of clues' poses as an instruction about the puzzle itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Slug and Lettuce is a chain of British bars, so it is an example of a pub.

clue.text: 25 pleading insanity having admitted tricky pastime?

indicators.note: having admitted means letting something in, so one piece goes inside the other
insanity suggests madness, so the letters of pleading are scrambled

parts.note: whist is a card game played by winning tricks, so it is a pastime full of tricks

explanation.surface: Someone pleads insanity in court after confessing to a cunning hobby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pleading insanity' looks like a legal defence; it is anagram fodder and signal. 'tricky' is a pun on tricks in card games.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pig and Whistle is a traditional British pub name, so it is an example of a pub.

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', a link word, so the definition is the noun congregation

parts.note: an Eccles cake is a currant pastry from Lancashire

indicators.note: in a down clue, risen means the letters are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-rate or perfect, written AI in crosswords

explanation.surface: A church congregation finds its cake perfect once it has risen in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: The cake is named after a town near Manchester. A1, meaning first-rate, is written with the letter I for the figure 1, then 'when risen' turns it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecclesia is the Greek word for an assembly, used for a church congregation.

clue.text: Resort central in remark of lower resort

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the cow's remark

parts.note: a lower here is a cow, one that lows, and its remark is a moo

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so the letters of central are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some central resort is mentioned by a resort further down the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lower' reads as 'more low' but is something that lows, a cow. 'Resort' at the start is re-sort, scrambling CENTRAL into NTECARL, which goes 'in' MOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Monte Carlo in Monaco is a famous casino and seaside holiday destination, so it is an example of a resort.

indicators.note: keeping means holding inside, so the rings go within the shortened slang word
endlessly means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: uncle is old British slang for a pawnbroker
O looks like a ring, so two rings are OO

explanation.surface: A pawnbroker keeps going on about rings he has taken out of pawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncle' as slang for a pawnbroker is old British usage. 'out' looks like part of 'rings out' but is the definition: unfashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Out as in out of fashion is a synonym for the slang adjective meaning unfashionable.

clue.text: Cold lake embraced by stupid swimmer

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: embraced by means held inside, so the lake's letter goes within the word for stupid

parts.note: oafish means clumsy and stupid
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A cold lake is surrounded by a dim-witted swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraced by' puts L inside OAFISH, giving OALFISH, after C.
explanation.definitionFit: A coalfish is the saithe, a North Atlantic fish, and any fish is a swimmer.

definitions.meaning: a pub, a common pub name being the ...
the royal headwear worn by six British kings named George, George I to George VI

explanation.walkthrough: The 6 is the number six, not a cross-reference to 6-down.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crown is a common pub name, and the British crown was worn by six Kings George.

indicators.note: allow frames the instruction: permitting a limited set of notes is the flip side of prohibiting the one left out

parts.note: the musical scale runs A to G, so a range stopping at F leaves out only the seventh note

explanation.surface: A news report proposes letting musicians play only the notes A to F.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay backwards: an instruction to prohibit G would, if obeyed, allow only notes A to F. 'suggesting' is a link word; the definition 'Report' is the noise of a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is the noise of a gun, a sudden loud explosion.

clue.text: Release sailor — there you have it!

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a common abbreviation for a sailor
said when presenting the answer to a problem, its resolution

explanation.surface: A sailor is freed, and that settles the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: AB stands for able-bodied seaman. 'there you have it!' is what one says on revealing the answer to a puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Absolution is a priest's formal release of a penitent from sin.

clue.text: 25 party terrific without right — then get down

parts.note: a do is British slang for a party

indicators.note: without means the letter for right is removed

parts.note: grand means terrific, as in 'a grand day out'
to duck is to get down quickly to avoid something

explanation.surface: A terrific party, then everyone has to take cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' as a noun for a party is British slang, and 'grand' meaning terrific is informal British.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dog and Duck is a traditional British pub name, so it is an example of a pub.

indicators.note: latest means the final letter of the word Bell is taken
made-up means invented or reworked, so the letters of cast are rearranged

parts.note: all means everyone

explanation.surface: The final bell rings and the actors, in stage make-up, are summoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latest' takes L from Bell; 'made-up' rearranges CAST into ASTC; ALL ends it. As a whole, the clue describes the publican's bell calling everyone for final drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Last call is the final chance to order drinks before a bar closes, signalled by a bell to all customers.

clue.text: Crash helmet needed when lacked control restraining child

indicators.note: restraining means holding in, so the child goes inside the word for lacked control

parts.note: a vehicle that slid skidded out of control
a kid is a child

explanation.surface: A crash helmet was needed when the rider lost control while holding a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed when' is link words. 'Skid lid' is British slang for a motorcycle helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: Skid lid is British slang for a motorcyclist's protective headgear.

clue.text: Still single, crowd in the distance

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one, means single

indicators.note: in places the crowd inside the distance

parts.note: a mile is a distance
a mob is a crowd

explanation.surface: Still unmarried, someone sees a crowd far away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like 'yet'; it means motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Still and motionless are synonyms, both describing something not moving.

clue.text: Where to go when three blocking road

indicators.note: blocking means standing in the way, so three goes inside the road

parts.note: a lane is a narrow road
tri- is the prefix meaning three

explanation.surface: Where can you go when three people are standing in the road?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where to go' is a euphemism for a toilet; 'when' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A latrine is a basic toilet, the place one goes to relieve oneself.

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: nags means pesters or worries
the head is the foam on top of a poured beer

explanation.surface: Worries over the foam on a pint of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' places NAGS above HEAD in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nag's Head is a traditional British pub name, so it is an example of a pub.

clue.text: In Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan etc, or it's in the north and south of East London?

definitions.text: it's in the north and south of East London
definitions.note: north and south is Cockney rhyming slang for mouth, so this is something found in a mouth

parts.note: the CIS, Commonwealth of Independent States, groups former Soviet republics such as these

explanation.surface: A geography quiz question about Central Asia, or about a part of East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang, from East London, uses 'north and south' for mouth, so the question asks for something in the mouth. 'north and south' looks like compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: An incisor is a front cutting tooth, and teeth are found in the mouth.

definitions.meaning: a pub, a common pub name being the ...
the lit walking figure on a British pedestrian crossing that shows it is safe to cross

explanation.definitionFit: The Green Man is a traditional pub name and also the walking-figure light at British crossings.

indicators.note: in places that letter inside the meeting

parts.note: a rally is a mass meeting

indicators.note: ultimately means the final letter of productive is taken

explanation.surface: A meeting that is ultimately very productive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ultimately' gives E from productive, which goes 'in' RALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Very and truly are synonyms used as intensifiers, as in 'it was very good'.

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the stuffing word goes round the abbreviation

parts.note: to gorge is to stuff oneself with food

explanation.surface: An English pub-goer stuffs his face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts GORGE around E.
explanation.definitionFit: The George is a common British pub name, usually after St George or a King George.

definitions.meaning: British slang for a quick glance, as in 'have a quick look'

explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for a glance and also names a male goose.

definitions.note: the definition is an adjective describing someone from the region

parts.note: nick and can are both slang for prison
ta is informal British for thanks
Brian is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A prisoner thanks a lad from the Spanish port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a name or theft; it is slang for prison, as is CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Santander is the capital of Cantabria in northern Spain, so a person from there is from that region.

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so both pieces are read backwards together

parts.note: L, from the Latin libra, is the symbol for the pound
had means got, as in 'had a present'

explanation.surface: A writer was offered money but turned it down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns LHAD into the writer's name. Roald Dahl wrote children's books; 'offered' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl was a British author of children's books such as Matilda.

definitions.meaning: the neighbourhood pub, where stout and other beers are drunk
read as low-cal, describing food or drink for dieters

explanation.definitionFit: The word means one's neighbourhood pub, and split as lo-cal it means low in calories, diet.

indicators.note: penetrates means goes inside, so firm and article go within the word for open

parts.note: overt means open and unconcealed
CO, short for company, means a firm
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A firm article tears through an open garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective describing the article, but it is the noun, a company.
explanation.definitionFit: An overcoat is a heavy coat, an example of a garment.
